author: assistant sub-agent V3G7 (v3 re-map); fix pass Fix2

vectors.enisa_quote: any existing communication link in the satellite lifecycle
vectors.reason: A communication link between the space and ground segments is the TT&C radio link; the interceptor is a receiver outside the mission, and ENISA adds that secondary/backup channels count.

vectors.enisa_quote: inside of specific segments - ground, space, user and human resources
vectors.reason: ENISA names links inside the ground segment (MOC to station, SLE/SDL), which an attacker taps from within ground systems.

review_response.finding: IA-0004 K-ENABLE (rf_link, enables EXF-0003) does not match SPARTA semantics
review_response.action: fixed: IA-0004 is now D-UNDESCRIBED; the backup-channel wording is carried by the EXF-0003.02 enisa_quote and the rf_link vector, and the rf_link entry is IA-0008.01 (receiver of a rogue ground station).

review_response.finding: No origin for 'inside of specific segments - ground, space, user': space and user links excluded
review_response.action: fixed: added feeder_rf (weak, 'between the segments'), user_terminal (weak, user segment/VSAT) and crosslink (weak, space segment) vectors with entries IA-0008.01/IA-0008/IA-0003; proximity not added because ENISA names no nearby platform.

review_response.finding: EXF-0002.03 traffic analysis K-ACTION is stronger than the quote
review_response.action: fixed: demoted to D-UNDESCRIBED; traffic analysis reads metadata and node power, not the data ENISA says is intercepted.

review_response.finding: engine: passive capture needs a fake TC entry (review_arch V-8, C-4)
review_response.action: kept because the validator requires a kept entry per vector; EXF-0003* are link_only by default so the engine skips the enabler, which is the intended workaround.

review_response.finding: M2: crosslink, feeder_rf and user_terminal vectors only produced model-artefact differences
review_response.action: fixed: all three vectors removed; IA-0003 is D-UNDESCRIBED (passive ISL monitoring needs no compromised neighbour and has no SPARTA technique). rf_link and ground remain.

review_response.finding: M2: report must say interception is not stopped by the modelled authentication controls

scope_note: TR29 is confidentiality of data on links. Controls that would change the result (SDLS encryption, NDS/IP, IPsec on F1) are outside the model's current protection axes (review_arch C-4). Interception here is not stopped by the modelled authentication controls (SDLS authentication, anti-replay); passive monitoring of crosslinks is not in the model (no SPARTA technique, no passive origin), and the feeder and service links are not mapped because ENISA names no such link.

rows.enisa_quote: Interception of data over a communication channel
rows.sparta_quote: captures mission traffic in transit, on ground networks or over the space link
rows.reason: Capturing mission traffic on a ground LAN, the space link or a crosslink is the interception ENISA names.

rows.enisa_quote: any existing communication link in the satellite lifecycle
rows.sparta_quote: By receiving or tapping the uplink path, the adversary collects telecommand frames
rows.reason: Tapping the ground-to-space command path is interception of one existing link; its content is telecommand frames.

rows.enisa_quote: primary and secondary commincation channels (e.g. used as backup)
rows.sparta_quote: The attacker records spacecraft-to-ground traffic, real-time telemetry
rows.reason: Recording spacecraft-to-ground telemetry and payload traffic is interception of the downlink, including backup channels.

rows.sparta_quote: Adversaries may field their own ground system, transportable or fixed, to transmit and receive mission-compatible signals
rows.reason: A rogue receiving/transmitting ground station is the equipment outside the mission that listens on the TT&C link.

rows.sparta_quote: any actor-controlled transmitter, platform, or node, ground, maritime, airborne, or space-based
rows.reason: An actor-controlled node outside the authorised architecture is the attacker's vantage point on the TT&C link.

Passive interception of inter-satellite traffic does not need a compromised neighbour satellite, and SPARTA has no technique for passive crosslink monitoring; ENISA only says 'links inside the space segment'.
Interception on links inside the ground segment (MOC to station, SLE/SDL) needs a foothold in the ground systems that carry them.
Receiver design needs the link's band, modulation/coding and framing, which this reconnaissance collects.
Finding the non-TT&C channels is what lets the interception reach links beyond TT&C.
Eavesdropping reconnaissance is the passive capture setup; ENISA's interception is the exfiltration-side use of the same capture.
Capturing the command path to learn framing is the preparation for uplink interception.
Harvesting downlink telemetry and beacons is the preparation for downlink interception.
Own antennas, LNA and demodulator chain are what an outside receiver needs to intercept TT&C or feeder signals.
Jamming denies the link; TR29 is about reading the traffic, not suppressing it.
Switching on-board crypto-mode values hides state from monitoring; it captures nothing on a link.
Biasing the clock for evasion changes on-board time bases, unrelated to receiving a channel.
A spoofed ephemeris corrupts the position solution on board; ENISA describes reading data in transit.
Masquerading as a legitimate entity is impersonation, ENISA TR43's subject, not passive reading.
Replay re-sends captured traffic; it uses an interception's output but is an active injection ENISA does not describe.
Replaying command packets is injection that needs an authority path, not listening on the channel.
Replaying bus traffic acts inside the spacecraft; ENISA's interception is of communication links.
Geofence-driven execution is an on-board trigger and has no link-reading behaviour.
Disabling or bypassing encryption defeats the protection that the intercept faces; ENISA TR45 covers that step.
Safe-mode weak protections matter for command access; ENISA TR29 describes capture, not commanding.
Editing on-board routing tables modifies data; the threat here is reading it in transit.
Skewing the system clock modifies on-board values; not interception.
Feeding erroneous input to receivers is a flood or confusion attack, not capture.
Spoofing sends forged signals; ENISA TR54 is the spoofing threat.
Time spoofing forges the time source and does not read any channel.
Spoofing bus traffic acts on the on-board bus, not on a communication link between segments.
GNSS-style spoofing is a signal-forgery attack described by ENISA TR54.
Side-channel attacks extract secrets from computation byproducts; SV-CF-1 lists it but ENISA says interception over a channel.
Jamming is link denial (TR44), not data capture.
Uplink jamming denies commanding; capture of the uplink is EXF-0003.01.
Downlink jamming denies telemetry; capture of the downlink is EXF-0003.02.
GNSS-band jamming is not the communication channel ENISA says is intercepted.
Replay-as-exfiltration induces new transmissions by sending commands; ENISA describes passive capture.
Side-channel exfiltration reads physical byproducts, not data carried on a communication channel.
Power-analysis attacks need hardware proximity or probing and do not describe link interception.
Electromagnetic leakage is read near the emitter; ENISA names communication links.
Traffic analysis reads flow metadata and node power profile, not the intercepted data; ENISA's 'any information' sentence is the generic consequence.
Timing attacks infer secrets from response latency, a different behaviour from capturing channel content.
Thermal imaging observes heat, which is no communication channel.
Co-opting a secondary link to carry stolen data out is exfiltration over an alternative channel, ENISA TR38.
A nearby vehicle collecting emissions is the proximity spying ENISA TR18 describes.
Reconfiguring a transponder to forward data to attacker receivers is exfiltration by reconfiguration, ENISA TR38.
Routing data out through an implanted payload channel is described with malicious injection in ENISA TR46.
Supply-chain insertion happens before flight and has no link-interception behaviour.
Poisoned dependencies and tools affect the built software, not a communication channel.
Malicious software introduced through the supply chain is ENISA TR55.
Hardware tampering before delivery is not capture of traffic on a link.
A compromised on-board SDR could mirror traffic, but ENISA does not describe tampering with the radio itself.
A backup-channel access path is for commanding; the ENISA words on secondary channels say a backup link can be intercepted too, which EXF-0003 already covers.
Compromising a backup ground station gives command access; interception on ground links needs only IA-0007.
Abusing the spacecraft's backup receiver is command injection, not listening.
Rendezvous is the proximity attacker's entry; ENISA TR29 names communication links and no nearby platform.
Emanation analysis reads leakage near the emitter, not a communication link.
A docked vehicle is a physical access path that ENISA does not mention here.
Grappling is a physical contact attack and unrelated to channel interception.
The hosted-payload door is an access path into the host bus; ENISA gives no such actor.
Manipulating the update pipeline implants software, ENISA TR46.
Commanding the spacecraft through a valid ground station is control seizure (TR52), not interception.
A rogue spacecraft as listener sits in the proximity/crosslink origin; ENISA TR29 names none, and the crosslink vector is modelled through IA-0003.
An ASAT weapon is a destructive actor, not a listener.
A trusted-relationship foothold is not one of the links ENISA names.
Collaborator access is an access path to systems, not interception of a link.
Vendor remote access is an access path to systems, not interception of a link.
A compromised user domain used as springboard goes into mission cores; interception on the user link is covered by the rogue terminal IA-0008.
Safe-mode access is a commanding technique and has no capture role.
Auxiliary-device compromise is an on-board access path, unrelated to links.
ATLO compromise is a pre-flight path; ENISA TR29 is about links.
Compromise of a host spacecraft is an access path from hosted functions, not interception.
Abusing native functionality is an on-board impact; interception leaves the spacecraft unchanged.
State or mode manipulation changes the spacecraft; TR29 only copies information.
Changing configuration is parameter modification (TR57).
Altering data is ENISA TR39; TR29 is confidentiality only.
Flow manipulation alters or redirects traffic; interception reads it without changing the flow.
Changing software or firmware is ENISA TR42.
Resource exhaustion is a denial-of-service outcome (TR51).
Timing manipulation changes the spacecraft; TR29 has confidentiality impact only.
Pivoting from a hosted payload is lateral movement to the bus; ENISA gives no such step.
Exploiting bus segregation is movement, not capture of a communication link.
Hopping to a neighbour needs control of the crosslink; intercepting traffic on it needs only IA-0003.
Rideshare-payload movement is a pivot between co-hosted payloads; ENISA describes none.
Replacing keys to cement control is part of the seizure TR52 describes.
Renting commercial ground-station time is a way to get an antenna; ENISA describes owned or tapped links, so RD-0001.01 is the needed preparation.
Obtaining keys prepares decryption of captured traffic, a later step ENISA does not describe.
Staging capabilities is generic preparation for later exploits, not for capture.
Staging an upload exploit prepares commanding, not listening.
Cryptographic-algorithm discovery prepares decryption, not the capture ENISA describes.
Commanding details prepare command injection; interception needs only link parameters.
ENISA's MFA example is something that gets intercepted; credential reconnaissance is a later use of the stolen secret.
Observing from a nearby platform is the proximity case that TR29 does not name.
Active scanning sends probes to elicit responses; ENISA's interception is passive reception.
Monitoring for safe-mode indicators prepares timing of command access, not capture.
